title: Opera Game
intro: Paul Morphy mates the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard in seventeen moves after they leave their king in the center and fall behind in development. The game is the usual classroom example of opening lines and using every piece.
hook: A queen sacrifice mates two consulting aristocrats in seventeen moves.

[Black "Duke of Brunswick & Count Isouard"]
[Result "1-0"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 Nf6 7. Qb3 Qe7
8. Nc3 c6 9. Bg5 b5 10. Nxb5 cxb5 11. Bxb5+ Nbd7 12. O-O-O Rd8 13. Rxd7 Rxd7
14. Rd1 Qe6 15. Bxd7+ Nxd7 16. Qb8+ Nxb8 17. Rd8# 1-0

plies.comment: White already has both bishops and the queen aiming at the uncastled king.
10.Nxb5 gives a piece to rip open the queenside. Black’s extra knight never gets into the game.
Both rooks occupy the open d-file. Black’s king is still on e8.
16.Qb8+ forces the last defender off d7.
The remaining rook mates on the back rank. Every white piece took part; the black queenside never moved.

title: Immortal Game
intro: Adolf Anderssen beats Lionel Kieseritzky by sacrificing both rooks and the queen and mating with bishop and knights. The finish is the reason nineteenth-century attacking chess still gets taught from this score.
hook: Anderssen gives both rooks and the queen, then mates with three minor pieces.

intro: Thirteen-year-old Bobby Fischer beats Donald Byrne after 17...Be6, offering the queen to keep a knight and bishop attacking the uncastled king. The rest is a series of checks that pick the position clean.
hook: Thirteen-year-old Fischer gives a queen and mates with a windmill of checks.

title: Deep Blue vs Kasparov, 1997
intro: Deep Blue wins the 1997 rematch in game six after Kasparov’s Caro-Kann walks into 8.Nxe6. The game is short and ugly, and it is the one people cite when they date the moment a computer beat the world champion in a match.
hook: Game six of the rematch: a machine wins the match in nineteen moves.

hook: Fischer plays 1.c4 and wins a model Queen’s Gambit. Spassky applauded.
